Juvenile Eastern Pacific bonito (Sarda chiliensis) undergo a rapid yolk-sac resorption phase, with hatching typically occurring after only 5 days [ab = 5 days] when incubated at 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva carries a minimal wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0006 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0006 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of related scombrids such as Scomber japonicus. This modest initial mass reflects the small, buoyant eggs characteristic of pelagic spawners and imposes an energetic constraint on the early larval stage. The endotrophic larva is entirely dependent on its yolk reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that must occur before the point of no return. Eclosion marks the beginning of a vulnerable planktonic drift phase during which predation pressure is extremely high, favoring a rapid developmental tempo. Field observations confirm that this abbreviated incubation duration at the specified temperature is consistent across much of the species' range, although slight variation in hatching time has been noted in relation to local thermal conditions experienced by the drifting eggs.

As the fish progresses through the early teleost larva stage, growth is fuelled by the progressive absorption of yolk nutrients and later by the first capture of copepod nauplii. The exotrophic transition occurs when the mouth gape opens and retinal differentiation allows for prey detection. By the time the postflexion larva begins to develop fin rays, a clear trajectory toward the juvenile body plan is established. Sexual maturation in this species is linked to body size rather than age alone, with total length at puberty recorded at 47 centimeters [Lp = 47 centimeters]. Individuals attaining this fork length typically exhibit the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. This length-based threshold is a common feature among fast-growing epipelagic predators. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length–weight relationship derived for Sarda chiliensis, is approximately 1,340 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,340 grams], representing a substantial increase over the larval mass. Puberty generally occurs within the first two years of life for most of the population, though some slower-growing individuals may delay maturation by an additional season.

The ultimate total length of the species reaches 102 centimeters [Li = 102 centimeters] for the largest sexually mature adults, a size that places Sarda chiliensis among the larger members of the tribe Sardini in the eastern Pacific. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight attained by these individuals is approximately 13,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 13,500 grams], based on the allometric scaling relationship established for this stock. This rapid growth trajectory is supported by a piscivorous diet consisting primarily of anchoveta, squid, and small mackerel. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 6 years [am = 6 years] when measured under the prevailing thermal regime of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C], although some tagging studies suggest that a small fraction of individuals may survive into a seventh year. Lifespan in this species is constrained by high natural mortality rates during the juvenile and early adult stages, with senescence-related physiological decline becoming apparent only in the oldest age classes. The relationship between body size and age is well described by a von Bertalanffy growth curve fitted to otolith-derived age estimates from commercial landings in Mexican and Central American waters.

Reproductive output in this highly fecund species is considerable. A single gravid female can produce up to 1,223 eggs per day [Ri = up to 1,223 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season when water temperatures reach 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C], a pattern extrapolated from the closely related Atlantic bonito (Sarda sarda). This daily fecundity, maintained over a protracted spawning period that may last several months, results in a lifetime egg production that can exceed one million oocytes per individual. Females are batch spawners, releasing multiple clutches of pelagic eggs over the course of a single season to maximize the probability of larval survival. The spawning season in the eastern Pacific typically extends from late spring through early autumn, peaking when sea surface temperatures are warmest. The high fecundity per spawning event is a classical life-history strategy among scombrids, compensating for extremely high rates of egg and larval mortality in the planktonic environment. These observations are based on histological examination of ovaries from landed specimens.

The natural mortality of adult Sarda chiliensis is influenced by predation from larger tunas, billfish, and marine mammals, in addition to fishing pressure. Organismal death in the wild occurs through predation, starvation during periods of low prey abundance, and age-related physiological deterioration. The completion of the lifespan at around 6 years [am = around 6 years] under the thermal conditions of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C] places this species on the shorter-lived end of the scombrid spectrum when compared to the larger tunas, such as Thunnus albacares, which may live for more than a decade. However, this relatively compressed lifespan is offset by an early age at maturation and an exceptionally high reproductive rate, traits that confer demographic resilience in a variable pelagic environment. Population models indicate that the species can sustain moderate fishing mortality despite its short life expectancy, provided that spawning stock biomass remains above critical thresholds. Ongoing monitoring of length and age distributions in the fishery is essential for detecting shifts in life-history parameters that may signal overexploitation or environmental change.
